hints: Notice the low sublimation temperature of 178 C, what does that tell you about whether aluminium chloride is ionic or covalent?
Remember aluminium in $\text{AlCl}_3$ has only 6 electrons in its outer shell, so it can accept a lone pair to complete its octet by dimerising to $\text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$.
Focus on the two bridging chlorines, each one is covalent to one Al and dative to the other, so check which diagram gives one dative bond to each Al.
walkthrough:
**Use sublimation temperature to decide bonding type**

Solid aluminium chloride sublimes at only 178 C. That is very low for an ionic lattice.

This tells us the solid must be covalent molecular, not giant ionic $\text{Al}^{3+}(\text{Cl}^-)_3$.

**Work out why a dimer forms**

In monomeric $\text{AlCl}_3$, Al has only 3 covalent bonds and 6 outer electrons. It is electron deficient.

$$\text{Al} : 3 \text{ bonds} = 6e^-, \text{needs 2 more for octet}$$

**Build the $\text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$ dimer with dative bonds**

Two $\text{AlCl}_3$ units join together. Two Cl atoms become bridges, each donates a lone pair into the empty orbital on the other Al.

$$2\text{AlCl}_3 \rightleftharpoons \text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$$
Each Al becomes tetrahedral with 2 terminal Cl plus 2 bridging Cl, and each Al accepts exactly one dative bond.

**Check the arrow direction**

A dative bond arrow points from donor to acceptor, so from Cl to Al.

The top bridge is covalent to the left Al and dative to the right Al, while the bottom bridge is covalent to the right Al and dative to the left Al. Only one diagram shows this balanced arrangement.

options.A: Correct. This shows the $\text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$ dimer present in the vapour just above sublimation. Each Al has 4 bonds (tetrahedral) and a complete octet, with one covalent and one dative bond from the two bridging Cl atoms shared evenly between the two Al centres.
options.B: Incorrect. This also shows a dimer but the dative arrows are wrong. It would give one Al too many bonds and leave the other Al still electron deficient with only 6 electrons, which does not stabilise both centres.
options.C: Incorrect. This is monomeric trigonal planar $\text{AlCl}_3$. The monomer only forms at much higher temperatures when the dimer dissociates. At 178 C the vapour is mainly the dimer $\text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$, and the monomer would leave Al with an incomplete octet.
options.D: Incorrect. This shows ionic $\text{Al}^{3+}(\text{Cl}^-)_3$. An ionic lattice would have very high melting and boiling points, not sublime at 178 C. Aluminium chloride is covalent with polarisation by the small highly charged $\text{Al}^{3+}$ ion.
